An open hand. A real responsibility.
Faith has to meet the person in front of me.
I want following Christ to become visible in how I pay attention, share power and remain answerable. Sometimes that means helping. Sometimes it means a boundary that protects someone else.
Listen before I turn someone’s situation into my explanation. Separate what I know from what I am assuming.
Offer help without making submission its price. Accept a cost freely, and ask who else is being asked to carry it.
Give reasons. Hear an objection. Protect people from harm, and change course when the consequences call for it.

If my tools, explanations and beliefs ask for trust, I owe people ways to question them. These are some of the places where that responsibility becomes concrete.

children: THE FIELD / A PLACE TO PRACTISE
Where the question meets a situation
Someone asks for help. What do I owe them?
The Field begins with a workshop shift that needs covering. A private request. An uncertain reason. A problem that will still exist tomorrow.
I want to examine what a choice does now, what it teaches a relationship, and what it makes normal over time. You can bring a different judgment—and ask what the scenario leaves out.
One fictional encounter. Five choices. Room to disagree.
What is mine to do next?
I cannot wait until every explanation is complete to practise care. I can act with reasons, acknowledge what I don’t know, and remain responsible for repair.
A few things I’ve built. A few things I’m still trying to understand.

children: A fictional situation. A real kind of responsibility.
Mira asks privately for help covering an evening workshop shift. The freezer needs maintenance. The coordinator says there is no budget for cover. You have limits of your own.
The shift is uncovered, maintenance is overdue, and Mira has asked privately for help.
The coordinator says there is no budget. That is a report, rather than the whole explanation.
Why Mira needs to leave, who else can help, and whether the budget claim is complete.
Open a choice to examine possible consequences. Compare them in any order. These branches are authored possibilities, not predictions about real people.
Keep the reasons open to correction.
Consider Mira, the other workers and your own continuing capacity.
Ask whether the cost was freely accepted, quietly shifted or left invisible.
Acknowledge a specific harm, change the practice, and allow accountability and time. An apology alone does not erase history.
This first encounter supports reflection. It does not assess your standing or certify a morally correct answer. You can disagree with its assumptions or leave.
What changes when one of us changes?
Follow a fictional household through changing values, capacity and agreements. See how being heard and keeping commitments shape willingness to ask again.
